notes.front: In Copilot’s request handling, what is Fill-in-the-Middle (FIM)?
notes.back: A pre-processing technique that gives the model the code after the cursor as well as the code before it.
notes.explanation: Seeing both sides widens the model’s view of the context, which the 2025 Learn unit says makes suggestions more accurate and relevant.
notes.example: Like guessing a missing word in a sentence by reading the words on both sides of the gap, not just those before it.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “GitHub Copilot user prompt process flow” (2025), “1. Secure prompt transmission and context gathering”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In Copilot’s request handling, what is the proxy filter?
notes.back: A proxy server that screens traffic, blocking attempts to hack the request or to make the system reveal how the model produces suggestions.
notes.explanation: According to the 2025 Learn unit, the request reaches it once context has been gathered, before any content filtering.
notes.example: Like a building’s front desk that turns away anyone trying to talk their way into the server room.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “GitHub Copilot user prompt process flow” (2025), “2. Proxy filter”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In Copilot’s request handling, what is the toxicity filter?
notes.back: A content filter that screens out hateful, offensive or inappropriate material and personal data.
notes.explanation: The 2025 Learn unit has it act on the incoming request and again on the model’s generated output.
notes.example: Like a newsroom editor who strikes both abusive language and a stranger’s home address from a story.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “GitHub Copilot user prompt process flow” (2025), “3. Toxicity filtering”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In Copilot’s request handling, what is post-processing?
notes.back: The checks run on the model’s output before you see it: the toxicity filter, then the proxy server’s quality, security and ethics checks.
notes.explanation: Per the 2025 Learn unit, any part of a response that fails is cut short or thrown away.
notes.example: Like a quality inspector at the end of a production line who removes faulty items before they ship.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “GitHub Copilot user prompt process flow” (2025), “5. Post-processing and response validation”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the 2025 Learn account of Copilot’s data flow, what is the inbound flow?
notes.back: The steps that carry your request to the model: sending and context gathering, proxy filter, toxicity filtering, then code generation.
notes.explanation: The unit splits Copilot’s handling in two, because a request goes in and a suggestion comes back.
notes.example: Like a letter’s journey to the writer: posted, screened at the sorting office, then answered.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “GitHub Copilot user prompt process flow” (2025), “Inbound flow”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the 2025 Learn account of Copilot’s data flow, what is the outbound flow?
notes.back: The steps after the model responds: post-processing and validation, delivery with a feedback loop, then repeating for later requests.
notes.explanation: It mirrors the inbound flow: the response is filtered again on its way back to you.
notes.example: Like the reply letter’s journey back: checked before posting, delivered, then the next letter starts again.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “GitHub Copilot user prompt process flow” (2025), “Outbound flow”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is a model’s context window?
notes.back: The total amount of information the model can consider at one time when generating a response.
notes.explanation: Its size is fixed and measured in tokens, and it varies by model.
notes.example: Like a desk that holds only so many open papers: once full, older sheets have to make room.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, Managing context in GitHub Copilot CLI, “About the context window”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: The context window is the total amount of information that the AI model can consider at one time when generating a response. The context window has a fixed size, measured in tokens, that varies by model.

notes.front: What is fine-tuning a large language model?
notes.back: Training a pretrained model further on a smaller, task-specific dataset, while it keeps what it learned in pretraining.
notes.explanation: The 2025 Learn unit calls the smaller set the target dataset and the pretrained starting point the source model.
notes.example: Like a qualified doctor doing a short specialist course: the general training stays, a specialism is added.

notes.front: What is Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA)?
notes.back: A fine-tuning method that adds small trainable parts to each layer of a pretrained model and leaves the original model unchanged.
notes.explanation: The 2025 Learn unit says GitHub used this method, and that it saves time and resources compared with retraining everything.
notes.example: Like clipping a small adapter onto each shelf of a finished bookcase instead of rebuilding the bookcase.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “GitHub Copilot Large Language Models (LLMs)” (2025), “LoRA fine-tuning”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

image.alt: Diagram of the seven-step code suggestion lifecycle. Inbound flow: 1 secure sending and context gathering (cursor code, open tabs, Fill-in-the-Middle); 2 proxy filter, which blocks attempts to manipulate the system; 3 toxicity filtering of harmful content and personal data; 4 code generation by the large language model. Outbound flow: 5 post-processing and response validation, where the toxicity filter then the proxy checks run and failures are truncated or discarded; 6 suggestion delivery and feedback loop, where only answers that pass every filter reach you; 7 repeat for later requests, looping back to step 1.

D) The audit log deleted the history

notes.explanation: Messages, responses and tool results all accumulate in the window, and large tool output fills it fastest.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, Managing context in GitHub Copilot CLI, “About the context window”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Tool results can be especially large—for example, if a tool reads a long file or runs a command that produces extensive output. All of this accumulates in the context window. In a long or complex session, the context window can fill up.

notes.front: Why may Copilot Chat give lower-quality help in a less common programming language?
notes.back: Quality in each language depends on the volume and diversity of its training data.
notes.explanation: A well-represented language such as JavaScript is well supported; rarer ones may do worse.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, Application card: GitHub Copilot Chat, “7. Limitations”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: For each language, the quality of suggestions depends on the volume and diversity of training data. For example, JavaScript is well-represented and well-supported, while less common languages may yield lower-quality results.

notes.front: How can training data drawn from existing repositories affect Copilot Chat’s output?
notes.back: Biases and errors in that code can be carried into its suggestions.
notes.explanation: It may also lean towards certain languages or coding styles, giving suboptimal or incomplete code.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, Application card: GitHub Copilot Chat, “7. Limitations”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Training data drawn from existing code repositories may contain biases and errors that can be perpetuated by the tool.

notes.front: A team maintaining code in a rarely used language finds Copilot Chat’s suggestions weaker than in their JavaScript projects. What best explains this?
notes.back: A: less training data for the language.
notes.choices:
A) Less common languages have less training data, so results may be lower quality
B) Content exclusion is on
C) The proxy filter blocks rare languages
D) Their context window is too large
notes.choicesExplained: B removes chosen files from Copilot’s context; it does not depend on language. C: the proxy filter screens manipulation attempts, not languages. D: a larger window gives more room, not worse results.
notes.explanation: Suggestion quality follows the volume and diversity of training data per language.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, Application card: GitHub Copilot Chat, “7. Limitations”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: less common languages may yield lower-quality results.

notes.front: Full fine-tuning versus LoRA: what gets trained?
notes.back: Full fine-tuning trains all parts of the network. LoRA trains only small added parts, leaving the original model as it was.
notes.explanation: The 2025 Learn unit describes full fine-tuning as slow and resource-hungry, which LoRA avoids.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “GitHub Copilot Large Language Models (LLMs)” (2025), “LoRA fine-tuning”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Will Copilot use your indexed repository to train models?
notes.back: No.
notes.explanation: The index serves semantic code search for answers and tasks, not model training.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, Indexing repositories for GitHub Copilot, “Benefit of indexing repositories”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Copilot will not use your indexed repository for model training.

notes.front: Once a repository is indexed, which Copilot features can use the index?
notes.back: Copilot Chat in GitHub and Visual Studio Code, and Copilot cloud agent.
notes.explanation: First indexing of a large repository can take up to 60 seconds; later updates usually take seconds.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, Indexing repositories for GitHub Copilot, “About index creation and use”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Once an index has been created for a repository, it can be used by: * Copilot Chat in GitHub and Visual Studio Code * Copilot cloud agent

notes.front: A legal team fears that asking Copilot Chat about their private repository will add its code to model training. What is correct?
notes.back: A: the repository is indexed for answers, not used for training.
notes.choices:
A) Chat indexes the repository to improve answers, and the index is not used for model training
B) The repository is added to training data after 28 days
C) Chat cannot answer questions about private repositories
D) Indexing must be requested by an enterprise owner
notes.choicesExplained: B mixes in a chat retention figure; indexed repositories are not used for training. C: Chat answers in repository context using the index. D: indexing happens automatically when a conversation has a repository context.
notes.explanation: Indexing supports semantic code search in answers, and GitHub states the index is not used for training.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, Indexing repositories for GitHub Copilot, “Semantic code search in Copilot Chat”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: When you start a conversation with Copilot Chat that has a repository context, the repository is automatically indexed to improve context-enriched answers to your questions about the code's structure and logic

notes.front: With BYOK active, where do your chat requests and responses go?
notes.back: To your selected provider, and they may be subject to that provider’s retention and privacy policies.
notes.explanation: You also become responsible for things such as key security, usage costs and output validation.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, Application card: GitHub Copilot Chat, “Using Bring Your Own Key (BYOK)”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: When using BYOK, your prompts and responses are transmitted to your selected provider and may be subject to that provider's data retention and privacy policies.

notes.front: When Copilot Chat uses Bing web search, what does it send to Bing?
notes.back: A search query generated from your request and additional context.
notes.explanation: An enterprise administrator can enable or disable Bing; the query is governed by Microsoft’s Privacy Statement.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, Application card: GitHub Copilot Chat, “7. Limitations”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: When web search is used, the content of your prompt, along with additional context, is used to generate a Bing search query on your behalf.

notes.front: Where does a Copilot cloud agent session run, and who can see it?
notes.back: In an ephemeral GitHub-hosted environment; its log stays on GitHub.com, shared by default with people who can access the repository.
notes.explanation: The environment is destroyed when the session ends, but the log remains.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, About GitHub Copilot session data, “Sessions run on GitHub”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Copilot cloud agent sessions run in an ephemeral environment hosted by GitHub. The environment is destroyed when the session ends, but the session log remains available on GitHub.com. These sessions are shared by default and visible to people with access to the repository.

notes.front: If an administrator enables syncing of local Copilot sessions, can the administrator read your synced session data?
notes.back: No. Synced data is tied to your personal account and accessible only to you by default.
notes.explanation: Administrators control whether syncing is available, not access to its contents.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, About GitHub Copilot session data, “Privacy and sharing”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Synced session data is tied to your personal account and is accessible only to you by default. Administrators can control whether syncing is available, but enabling syncing does not give them access to your session data.
